headline: Botswana Honors 97-Year-Old Who Stood Against Indigenous Eviction
meta_description: Roy Sesana receives honorary doctorate for decades fighting to protect San people's rights to ancestral Kalahari lands, with new government backing his cause.
summary_short: At 97, Roy Sesana was honored by the University of Botswana for his lifelong fight to protect Indigenous San communities from removal from the Central Kalahari.
body:
Roy Sesana, a 97-year-old Indigenous rights campaigner, received an honorary Doctor of Letters from the University of Botswana on October 23, recognized for nearly four decades of advocacy defending San communities against forced removal from their ancestral lands in the Central Kalahari Game Reserve. The award marks a remarkable reversal: the man once branded as a "public enemy number one" by his own government for taking the state to court now stands honored by the nation's highest institutions. His legal victory came nearly 20 years ago when Botswana's High Court ruled in his favor, validating claims that San communities had been wrongfully displaced in the 1990s and early 2000s under the guise of conservation and service delivery.

The timing of this recognition carries deeper significance. Duma Boko, one of the lawyers who represented San communities in that landmark court case, is now Botswana's president. Since taking office in November 2024, Boko has prioritized Indigenous land rights, establishing an interministerial committee to address longstanding grievances and approving a plan in September 2026 to restore legally protected land rights across the 52,000-square-kilometer reserve. The government's vision allows communities to reclaim rights while keeping the reserve protected—a compromise Sesana helped make possible through decades of relentless advocacy.

Yet Sesana's humility tempers the celebration. He dedicated his honorary doctorate to the Basarwa people and all Botswanans, encouraging younger generations to preserve their cultural identity. But in interviews before the ceremony, he remained clear-eyed: the struggle for ancestral land and self-determination, he said, remains far from over. His decades-long fight demonstrates that persistence can bend even the most entrenched systems toward justice.

Central Kalahari Game Reserve: 52,000 square kilometers in Botswana
San communities displaced in 1990s and early 2000s
